3354: #### 2. Core system architecture
3355: 
3356: The Bluetooth Core system consists of a Host and a Controller. A minimal implementation of the Bluetooth BR/EDR core system covers the four lowest layers and associated protocols defined by the Bluetooth specification as well as one common service layer protocol; the Service Discovery Protocol (SDP) and the overall profile requirements are specified in the Generic Access Profile (GAP). A minimal implementation of a Bluetooth LE only core system covers the four lowest layers and associated protocols defined by the Bluetooth specification as well as two common service layer protocols; the Security Manager (SM) and Attribute Protocol (ATT) and the overall profile requirements are specified in the Generic Attribute Profile (GATT) and Generic Access Profile (GAP). Implementations combining Bluetooth BR/EDR and LE include both of the minimal implementations described above.
3357: 
3358: A complete Bluetooth application requires a number of additional service and higher layer protocols that are defined in the Bluetooth specification, but are not described here. The core system architecture is shown in [Figure 2.1](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e_figure-idm4640314047019233541872501872 "Figure 2.1: Bluetooth core system architecture ").

Link Manager, Link Controller and BR/EDR Radio blocks comprise a BR/EDR Controller. Link Manager, Link Controller and LE Radio blocks comprise an LE Controller. L2CAP, SDP and GAP blocks comprise a BR/EDR Host. L2CAP, SMP, Attribute Protocol, GAP and Generic Attribute Profile (GATT) blocks comprise an LE Host. A BR/EDR/LE Host combines the set of blocks from each respective Host. This is a common implementation involving a standard physical communication interface between the Controller and the Host. Although this interface is optional the architecture is designed to allow for its existence and characteristics. The Bluetooth specification enables interoperability between independent Bluetooth systems by defining the protocol messages exchanged between equivalent layers, and also interoperability between independent Bluetooth Controllers and Bluetooth Hosts by defining a common interface between Bluetooth Controllers and Bluetooth Hosts.
3368: 
3369: A number of functional blocks and the path of services and data between them are shown. The functional blocks shown in the diagram provide a set of conceptual entities that are used when describing the requirements of the specification; in general the Bluetooth specification does not define the details of implementations except where this is required for interoperability. Thus the functional blocks in [Figure 2.1](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e_figure-idm4640314047019233541872501872 "Figure 2.1: Bluetooth core system architecture ") are shown in order to aid description of the system behavior. An implementation may be different from the system shown in [Figure 2.1](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e_figure-idm4640314047019233541872501872 "Figure 2.1: Bluetooth core system architecture ").
3370: 
3371: Standard interactions are defined for all inter-device operation, where Bluetooth devices exchange protocol signaling according to the Bluetooth specification. The Bluetooth core system protocols are the Radio (PHY) protocol, Link Control (LC) and Link Manager (LM) protocol or Link Layer (LL) protocol, and Logical Link Control and Adaptation protocol (L2CAP), all of which are fully defined in subsequent parts of the Bluetooth specification. In addition, the Service Discovery protocol (SDP) and the Attribute Protocol (ATT) are service layer protocols that may be required by some Bluetooth applications.
3372: 
3373: The Bluetooth core system offers services through a number of service access points that are shown in the diagram as ellipses. These services consist of the basic primitives that control the Bluetooth core system. The services can be split into three types. There are device control services that modify the behavior and modes of a Bluetooth device, transport control services that create, modify and release traffic bearers (channels and links), and data services that are used to submit data for transmission over traffic bearers. It is common to consider the first two as belonging to the C-plane and the last as belonging to the U-plane.
3374: 
3375: A service interface to the Bluetooth Controller is defined such that the Controller may be considered a standard part. In this configuration the Bluetooth Controller operates the lowest four layers. The Bluetooth Host operates the L2CAP layer and other higher layers. The standard interface is called the Host Controller interface (HCI) and its service access points are represented by the ellipses on the upper edge of the Bluetooth Controller in [Figure 2.1](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e_figure-idm4640314047019233541872501872 "Figure 2.1: Bluetooth core system architecture "). Implementation of this standard service interface is optional.
3376: 
3377: As the Bluetooth architecture is defined with the possibility of separate Host and Controller(s) communicating through one or more HCI transports, a number of general assumptions are made. Bluetooth Controllers are assumed to have limited data buffering capabilities in comparison with the Host. Therefore the L2CAP layer is expected to carry out some simple resource management when submitting L2CAP PDUs to the Controller for transport to a peer device. This includes segmentation of L2CAP SDUs into more manageable PDUs and then the fragmentation of PDUs into start and continuation packets of a size suitable for the Controller buffers, and management of the use of Controller buffers to ensure availability for channels with Quality of Service (QoS) commitments.
3378: 
3379: The BR/EDR Baseband and LE Link Layer provide the basic acknowledgment/repeat request (ARQ) protocol in Bluetooth. The L2CAP layer may provide further error detection and retransmission to the L2CAP PDUs. This feature is recommended for applications with requirements for a low probability of undetected errors in the user data. A window-based flow control feature may be used to manage buffer allocation in the receiving device. Both of these optional features augment the QoS performance in certain scenarios. Not all of the L2CAP capabilities are available when using the LE system.
3380: 
3381: Although these assumptions are not always required for embedded Bluetooth implementations that combine all layers in a single system, the general architectural and QoS models are defined with these assumptions in mind, in effect a lowest common denominator.
3382: 
3383: Automated conformance testing of implementations of the Bluetooth core system is required. This is achieved by allowing a test system to control the implementation through the PHY interface, test interfaces such as Direct Test Mode (DTM), Unified Test Protocol (UTP), and test commands and events over HCI which are only required for conformance testing.
3384: 
3385: The test system is composed of an Upper Tester, which controls and observes the upper service boundary of the IUT, and a Lower Tester, which controls and observes the lower service boundary of the IUT. The Lower Tester exchanges messages with the implementation under test (IUT) through the PHY interface. The Upper Tester controls the IUT through HCI, DTM, UTP, or test commands. If the targeted layer of the test is the PHY layer, then the Upper Tester may use a BR/EDR or LE connection to control the IUT over the air.

3387: ##### 2.1. Core architectural blocks
3388: 
3389: This section describes the function and responsibility of each of the blocks shown in [Figure 2.1](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e_figure-idm4640314047019233541872501872 "Figure 2.1: Bluetooth core system architecture "). An implementation is not required to follow the architecture described above, though every implementation is still required to conform to the protocol specifications, behaviors, and other requirements specified in subsequent parts of the Bluetooth specification.
3390: 
3391: ###### 2.1.1. Host architectural blocks
3392: 
3393: ###### 2.1.1.1. Channel manager
3394: 
3395: The channel manager is responsible for creating, managing and closing L2CAP channels for the transport of service protocols and application data streams. The channel manager uses the L2CAP protocol to interact with a channel manager on a remote (peer) device to create these L2CAP channels and connect their endpoints to the appropriate entities. The channel manager interacts with its local link manager to create new logical links (if necessary) and to configure these links to provide the required quality of service for the type of data being transported.
3396: 
3397: ###### 2.1.1.2. L2CAP resource manager
3398: 
3399: The L2CAP resource manager block is responsible for managing the ordering of submission of PDU fragments to the baseband and some relative scheduling between channels to ensure that L2CAP channels with QoS commitments are not denied access to the physical channel due to Controller resource exhaustion. This is required because the architectural model does not assume that a Controller has limitless buffering, or that the HCI is a pipe of infinite bandwidth.
3400: 
3401: L2CAP Resource Managers may also carry out traffic conformance policing to check that applications are submitting L2CAP SDUs within the bounds of their negotiated QoS settings. The general Bluetooth data transport model assumes well-behaved applications, and does not define how an implementation is expected to deal with this problem.
3402: 
3403: ###### 2.1.1.3. Security Manager Protocol
3404: 
3405: The Security Manager Protocol (SMP) is the peer-to-peer protocol used to generate encryption keys and identity keys. The protocol operates over a dedicated fixed L2CAP channel. The SMP block also manages storage of the encryption keys and identity keys and is responsible for generating random addresses and resolving random addresses to known device identities. The SMP block interfaces with the Controller to provide stored keys used for encryption and authentication during the encryption or pairing procedures.
3406: 
3407: This block is only used in LE systems. Similar functionality in the BR/EDR system is contained in the Link Manager block in the Controller. SMP functionality is in the Host on LE systems to reduce the implementation cost of the LE only Controllers.
3408: 
3409: ###### 2.1.1.4. Attribute Protocol
3410: 
3411: The Attribute Protocol (ATT) block implements the peer-to-peer protocol between an ATT Server and an ATT Client. The ATT Client communicates with an ATT Server on a remote device over a dedicated fixed L2CAP channel. The ATT Client sends commands, requests, and confirmations to the ATT Server. The ATT Server sends responses, notifications and indications to the client. These ATT Client commands and requests provide a means to read and write values of attributes on a peer device with an ATT Server.
3412: 
3413: ###### 2.1.1.5. \[This section is no longer used\]
3414: 
3415: ###### 2.1.1.6. Generic Attribute Profile
3416: 
3417: The Generic Attribute Profile (GATT) block represents the functionality of the ATT Server and, optionally, the ATT Client. The profile describes the hierarchy of services, characteristics and attributes used in the ATT Server. The block provides interfaces for discovering, reading, writing and indicating of service characteristics and attributes. GATT is used on LE devices for LE profile service discovery.
3418: 
3419: ###### 2.1.1.7. Generic Access Profile
3420: 
3421: The Generic Access Profile (GAP) block represents the base functionality common to all Bluetooth devices such as modes and access procedures used by the transports, protocols and application profiles. GAP services include device discovery, connection modes, security, authentication, association models and service discovery.
3422: 
3423: ###### 2.1.1.8. Service Discovery Protocol
3424: 
3425: The Service Discovery Protocol (SDP) provides a mechanism to allow clients to search for needed services based on specific attributes of the service, including search based on class of service and browsing the entire database. SDP is used on BR/EDR devices for BR/EDR profile service discovery.
3426: 
3427: SDP focuses on discovering services available from or through Bluetooth devices. It does not define methods for accessing services once they are discovered with SDP; the access method is service-specific.
3428: 
3429: ###### 2.1.2. BR/EDR/LE Controller architectural blocks
3430: 
3431: In implementations where the BR/EDR and LE systems are combined, the architectural blocks may be shared between systems or each system may have their own instantiation of the block.
3432: 
3433: ###### 2.1.2.1. Device manager
3434: 
3435: The device manager is the functional block in the baseband that controls the general behavior of the Bluetooth device. It is responsible for all operations of the Bluetooth system that are not directly related to data transport, such as inquiring for the presence of nearby Bluetooth devices, connecting to Bluetooth devices, or making the local Bluetooth device discoverable or connectable by other devices.
3436: 
3437: The device manager requests access to the transport medium from the baseband resource Controller in order to carry out its functions.
3438: 
3439: The device manager also controls local device behavior implied by a number of the HCI commands, such as managing the device local name, any stored link keys, and other functionality.
3440: 
3441: ###### 2.1.2.2. Link manager
3442: 
3443: The link manager is responsible for the creation, modification and release of logical links (and, if required, their associated logical transports), as well as the update of parameters related to physical links between devices. The link manager achieves this by communicating with the link manager in remote Bluetooth devices using the Link Manager Protocol (LMP) in BR/EDR and the Link Layer Protocol (LL) in LE.
3444: 
3445: The LM or LL protocol allows the creation of new logical links and logical transports between devices when required, as well as the general control of link and transport attributes such as the enabling of encryption on the logical transport, the adapting of transmit power on the physical link, or the adjustment of QoS settings in BR/EDR for a logical link.
3446: 
3447: ###### 2.1.2.3. Baseband resource manager
3448: 
3449: The baseband resource manager is responsible for all access to the radio medium. It has two main functions. At its heart is a scheduler that grants time on the physical channels to all of the entities that have negotiated an access contract. The other main function is to negotiate access contracts with these entities. An access contract is effectively a commitment to deliver a certain QoS that is required in order to provide a user application with an expected performance.
3450: 
3451: The access contract and scheduling function must take account of any behavior that requires use of the Controller. This includes (for example) the normal exchange of data between connected devices over logical links, and logical transports, as well as the use of the radio medium to carry out inquiries, make connections, be discoverable or connectable, or to take readings from unused carriers during the use of adaptive frequency hopping mode.
3452: 
3453: In some cases in BR/EDR systems the scheduling of a logical link results in changing a logical link to a different physical channel from the one that was previously used. This may be (for example) due to involvement in scatternet, a periodic inquiry function, or page scanning. When the physical channels are not time slot aligned, then the resource manager also accounts for the realignment time between slots on the original physical channel and slots on the new physical channel. In some cases the slots will be naturally aligned due to the same device clock being used as a reference for both physical channels.
3454: 
3455: ###### 2.1.2.4. Link Controller
3456: 
3457: The Link Controller is responsible for the encoding and decoding of Bluetooth packets from the data payload and parameters related to the physical channel, logical transport and logical link.
3458: 
3459: The Link Controller carries out the link control protocol signaling in BR/EDR and Link Layer protocol in LE (in close conjunction with the scheduling function of the resource manager), which is used to communicate flow control and acknowledgment and retransmission request signals. The interpretation of these signals is a characteristic of the logical transport associated with the baseband packet. Interpretation and control of the link control signaling is normally associated with the resource manager’s scheduler.
3460: 
3461: ###### 2.1.2.5. PHY
3462: 
3463: The PHY block is responsible for transmitting and receiving packets of information on the physical channel. A control path between the baseband and the PHY block allows the baseband block to control the timing and frequency carrier of the PHY block. The PHY block transforms a stream of data to and from the physical channel and the baseband into required formats.
3464: 
3465: ###### 2.1.2.6. Isochronous Adaptation Layer
3466: 
3467: The Isochronous Adaptation Layer (ISOAL) enables the upper layer to send or receive isochronous data to or from the Link Layer in a flexible way such that the size and interval of data packets in the upper layer can be different from the size and interval of data packets in the Link Layer. The ISOAL uses fragmentation/recombination or segmentation/reassembly operations to convert upper layer data units into lower layer data units (or the other way around).
3468: 
3469: ###### 2.1.2.7. Channel Sounding
3470: 
3471: The Channel Sounding block is responsible for creation, modification, and release of Channel Sounding physical links. Channel Sounding related capabilities are first exchanged between peer Channel Sounding blocks and procedure configuration parameters are established. Security parameters are then set up. Thereafter, Channel Sounding exchanges are coordinated via this block, which includes Channel Sounding event, subevent, and step timing. Step transmission and reception is also generated and coordinated through this block. This data is then sent to the Host. From these exchanges, data is collected that may be used by the Host for distance estimation and attack detection.

蓝牙核心系统由一个主机和一个控制器组成。蓝牙 BR/EDR 核心系统的最小实现涵盖蓝牙规范定义的四个最低层及其相关协议，以及一个通用服务层协议；服务发现协议（SDP）和整体配置文件要求在通用访问配置文件（GAP）中规定。仅 LE 的蓝牙核心系统的最小实现涵盖蓝牙规范定义的四个最低层及其相关协议，以及两个通用服务层协议；安全管理器（SM）和属性协议（ATT）以及整体配置文件要求在通用属性配置文件（GATT）和通用访问配置文件（GAP）中规定。结合蓝牙 BR/EDR 和 LE 的实现包含上述两种最小实现。

完整的蓝牙应用需要蓝牙规范中定义但此处未描述的许多附加服务和更高层协议。核心系统架构如[图 2.1](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e_figure-idm4640314047019233541872501872 "图 2.1：蓝牙核心系统架构 ") 所示。

图中展示了多个功能模块以及它们之间服务和数据的路径。图中所示的功能模块提供了一组概念实体，用于描述规范的要求；通常，蓝牙规范不定义实现的细节，除非出于互操作性需要。因此，[图 2.1](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e_figure-idm4640314047019233541872501872 "图 2.1：蓝牙核心系统架构 ") 中所示的功能模块是为了辅助描述系统行为而展示的。实现可能与 [图 2.1](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e_figure-idm4640314047019233541872501872 "图 2.1：蓝牙核心系统架构 ") 中所示的系统不同。

为所有设备间操作定义了标准交互，其中蓝牙设备根据蓝牙规范交换协议信令。蓝牙核心系统协议包括射频（PHY）协议、链路控制（LC）和链路管理器（LM）协议或链路层（LL）协议，以及逻辑链路控制与适配协议（L2CAP），所有这些都在蓝牙规范的后续部分中有完整定义。此外，服务发现协议（SDP）和属性协议（ATT）是某些蓝牙应用可能需要的服务层协议。

蓝牙核心系统通过多个服务访问点提供服务，这些服务访问点在图中以椭圆表示。这些服务由控制蓝牙核心系统的基本原语组成。服务可分为三种类型。有修改蓝牙设备行为和模式的设备控制服务，创建、修改和释放流量承载（信道和链路）的传输控制服务，以及用于提交数据以便在流量承载上传输的数据服务。通常将前两者视为属于 C 平面，将最后一个视为属于 U 平面。

定义了到蓝牙控制器的服务接口，使得控制器可以被视为一个标准部件。在这种配置中，蓝牙控制器运行最低四层。蓝牙主机运行 L2CAP 层和其他更高层。该标准接口称为主机控制器接口（HCI），其服务访问点由 [图 2.1](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e_figure-idm4640314047019233541872501872 "图 2.1：蓝牙核心系统架构 ") 中蓝牙控制器上边缘的椭圆表示。该标准服务接口的实现是可选的。

由于蓝牙架构定义中存在独立的主机和控制器通过一个或多个 HCI 传输进行通信的可能性，因此做出了一些一般性假设。假设蓝牙控制器与主机相比具有有限的数据缓冲能力。因此，L2CAP 层在向控制器提交 L2CAP PDU 以便传输到对端设备时，应执行一些简单的资源管理。这包括将 L2CAP SDU 分段为更易于管理的 PDU，然后将 PDU 分片为适合控制器缓冲区大小的起始和续传数据包，以及管理控制器缓冲区的使用以确保具有服务质量（QoS）承诺的信道可用。

BR/EDR 基带和 LE 链路层提供蓝牙中的基本确认/重传请求（ARQ）协议。L2CAP 层可对 L2CAP PDU 提供进一步的错误检测和重传。建议对用户数据中未检测错误概率有低要求的应用使用此特性。可使用基于窗口的流控制特性来管理接收设备中的缓冲区分配。这两个可选特性在某些场景下增强了 QoS 性能。使用 LE 系统时，并非所有 L2CAP 功能都可用。

虽然对于将所有层组合在单个系统中的嵌入式蓝牙实现，这些假设并不总是必需的，但通用架构和 QoS 模型是在考虑这些假设的情况下定义的，实际上是一个最低公共标准。

需要对蓝牙核心系统实现进行自动一致性测试。这是通过允许测试系统通过 PHY 接口、诸如直接测试模式（DTM）、统一测试协议（UTP）等测试接口，以及仅在一致性测试时需要的 HCI 上的测试命令和事件来控制实现而实现的。

测试系统由上层测试器和下层测试器组成，前者控制和观察 IUT 的上层服务边界，后者控制和观察 IUT 的下层服务边界。下层测试器通过 PHY 接口与被测实现（IUT）交换消息。上层测试器通过 HCI、DTM、UTP 或测试命令控制 IUT。如果测试的目标层是 PHY 层，则上层测试器可使用 BR/EDR 或 LE 连接通过空中接口控制 IUT。

##### 2.1. 核心架构模块

本节描述 [图 2.1](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e_figure-idm4640314047019233541872501872 "图 2.1：蓝牙核心系统架构 ") 中所示每个模块的功能和职责。实现不需要遵循上述架构，但每个实现仍需符合蓝牙规范后续部分中规定的协议规范、行为和其他要求。

###### 2.1.1. 主机架构模块

###### 2.1.1.1. 信道管理器

信道管理器负责创建、管理和关闭用于传输服务协议和应用数据流的 L2CAP 信道。信道管理器使用 L2CAP 协议与远程（对端）设备上的信道管理器交互，以创建这些 L2CAP 信道并将其端点连接到适当的实体。信道管理器与其本地链路管理器交互以创建新的逻辑链路（如有必要），并配置这些链路以便为所传输的数据类型提供所需的服务质量。

###### 2.1.1.2. L2CAP 资源管理器

L2CAP 资源管理器模块负责管理向基带提交 PDU 分片的顺序以及信道之间的一些相对调度，以确保具有 QoS 承诺的 L2CAP 信道不会因控制器资源耗尽而被拒绝访问物理信道。这是必需的，因为架构模型不假设控制器具有无限的缓冲，也不假设 HCI 是无限带宽的管道。

L2CAP 资源管理器还可执行流量一致性监管，以检查应用是否在其协商的 QoS 设置范围内提交 L2CAP SDU。通用蓝牙数据传输模型假设应用行为良好，并且不定义实现应如何处理此问题。

###### 2.1.1.3. 安全管理器协议

安全管理器协议（SMP）是用于生成加密密钥和身份密钥的对等协议。该协议在专用的固定 L2CAP 信道上运行。SMP 模块还管理加密密钥和身份密钥的存储，并负责生成随机地址以及将随机地址解析为已知设备身份。SMP 模块与控制器接口，以在加密或配对过程中提供用于加密和认证的已存储密钥。

此模块仅在 LE 系统中使用。BR/EDR 系统中的类似功能包含在控制器的链路管理器模块中。LE 系统中的 SMP 功能位于主机中，以降低仅 LE 控制器的实现成本。

###### 2.1.1.4. 属性协议

属性协议（ATT）模块实现 ATT 服务器和 ATT 客户端之间的对等协议。ATT 客户端通过专用的固定 L2CAP 信道与远程设备上的 ATT 服务器通信。ATT 客户端向 ATT 服务器发送命令、请求和确认。ATT 服务器向客户端发送响应、通知和指示。这些 ATT 客户端命令和请求提供了一种手段，用于读取和写入具有 ATT 服务器的对端设备上的属性值。

###### 2.1.1.6. 通用属性配置文件

通用属性配置文件（GATT）模块表示 ATT 服务器的功能，以及可选的 ATT 客户端的功能。该配置文件描述了 ATT 服务器中使用的服务、特征和属性的层次结构。该模块提供用于发现、读取、写入和指示服务特征和属性的接口。GATT 用于 LE 设备上的 LE 配置文件服务发现。

###### 2.1.1.7. 通用访问配置文件

通用访问配置文件（GAP）模块表示所有蓝牙设备共有的基础功能，例如传输、协议和应用配置文件使用的模式和访问过程。GAP 服务包括设备发现、连接模式、安全、认证、关联模型和服务发现。

###### 2.1.1.8. 服务发现协议

服务发现协议（SDP）提供一种机制，允许客户端根据服务的特定属性搜索所需服务，包括基于服务类别的搜索和浏览整个数据库。SDP 用于 BR/EDR 设备上的 BR/EDR 配置文件服务发现。

SDP 专注于发现可从蓝牙设备获得或通过蓝牙设备获得的服务。它不定义通过 SDP 发现服务后访问服务的方法；访问方法是特定于服务的。

###### 2.1.2. BR/EDR/LE 控制器架构模块

在 BR/EDR 和 LE 系统组合的实现中，架构模块可在系统之间共享，或者每个系统可有自己的模块实例。

###### 2.1.2.1. 设备管理器

设备管理器是基带中控制蓝牙设备一般行为的功能模块。它负责蓝牙系统中所有与数据传输不直接相关的操作，例如查询附近蓝牙设备的存在、连接到蓝牙设备、或使本地蓝牙设备可被其他设备发现或可连接。

设备管理器向基带资源控制器请求访问传输介质以执行其功能。

设备管理器还控制由多个 HCI 命令隐含的本地设备行为，例如管理设备本地名称、任何已存储的链路密钥以及其他功能。

###### 2.1.2.2. 链路管理器

链路管理器负责创建、修改和释放逻辑链路（以及如有需要，其相关联的逻辑传输），以及更新与设备之间物理链路相关的参数。链路管理器通过在 BR/EDR 中使用链路管理器协议（LMP）和在 LE 中使用链路层协议（LL）与远程蓝牙设备中的链路管理器通信来实现这一点。

LM 或 LL 协议允许在需要时在设备之间创建新的逻辑链路和逻辑传输，以及对链路和传输属性的一般控制，例如在逻辑传输上启用加密、在物理链路上调整发射功率，或在 BR/EDR 中为逻辑链路调整 QoS 设置。

###### 2.1.2.3. 基带资源管理器

基带资源管理器负责对射频介质的所有访问。它有两个主要功能。其核心是一个调度器，向所有已协商访问合约的实体授予物理信道上的时间。另一个主要功能是与这些实体协商访问合约。访问合约实际上是交付特定 QoS 的承诺，该 QoS 是为用户应用提供预期性能所必需的。

访问合约和调度功能必须考虑需要使用控制器的任何行为。这包括（例如）连接设备之间通过逻辑链路和逻辑传输进行的正常数据交换，以及使用射频介质执行查询、建立连接、可发现或可连接，或在自适应跳频模式使用期间从未使用的载波获取读数。

在 BR/EDR 系统中，某些情况下逻辑链路的调度会导致将逻辑链路切换到与先前使用的不同的物理信道。这可能（例如）是由于参与散射网、周期性查询功能或寻呼扫描。当物理信道在时隙上未对齐时，资源管理器还要考虑原始物理信道上的时隙与新物理信道上的时隙之间的重新对齐时间。在某些情况下，由于两个物理信道使用相同的设备时钟作为参考，时隙将自然对齐。

###### 2.1.2.4. 链路控制器

链路控制器负责根据数据有效载荷以及与物理信道、逻辑传输和逻辑链路相关的参数对蓝牙数据包进行编码和解码。

链路控制器执行 BR/EDR 中的链路控制协议信令和 LE 中的链路层协议（与资源管理器的调度功能密切配合），用于传达流控制以及确认和重传请求信号。这些信号的解释是与基带数据包相关联的逻辑传输的特征。链路控制信令的解释和控制通常与资源管理器的调度器相关联。

###### 2.1.2.5. PHY

PHY 模块负责在物理信道上发送和接收信息数据包。基带和 PHY 模块之间的控制路径允许基带模块控制 PHY 模块的定时和频率载波。PHY 模块将物理信道和基带之间的数据流转换为所需格式。

###### 2.1.2.6. 等时适配层

等时适配层（ISOAL）使上层能够以灵活的方式向链路层发送或从链路层接收等时数据，使得上层中数据包的大小和间隔可以与链路层中数据包的大小和间隔不同。ISOAL 使用分片/重组或分段/重装操作将上层数据单元转换为下层数据单元（或反之）。

###### 2.1.2.7. 信道探测

信道探测（CS）模块负责创建、修改和释放信道探测物理链路。首先在对等的信道探测模块之间交换与信道探测相关的能力，并建立过程配置参数。然后设置安全参数。此后，通过此模块协调信道探测交换，包括信道探测事件、子事件和步骤定时。步骤的发送和接收也通过此模块生成和协调。然后将此数据发送到主机。从这些交换中收集的数据可由主机用于距离估计和攻击检测。
